source.title: Compressed Computation under $L^4$ Loss is likely Computation in Superposition
source.citation: Francisco Ferreira da Silva et al., 2026
source.authors: Francisco Ferreira da Silva; S. Heimersheim

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. There are minor extraction and math-formatting artifacts, but the results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests superposition in a toy network using a compressed-computation task and a loss-exponent sweep, rather than reproducing the original representation-superposition method.
record.gate_note: The study reports results for a trained 100-feature, 50-neuron network, its code geometry and decoder, and variants with different loss exponents and model sizes. The stated input sparsity p = 0.02 is a setting, not a sparsity-sweep result. The paper also cites prior results; those are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains a toy ReLU network with more sparse features (100) than neurons (50). It reports whether features come to share neurons through overlapping, regular sparse codes, and under which loss this happens. That bears on V1, and weakly on V2, in a new setting: computation rather than representation. The L4 loss is an ordinary training objective, not a reward built for superposition. Still, the authors chose it to elicit the solution, and L2 does not produce it.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue, hedged as 'likely', that L4 (and any exponent >2) training elicits computation in superposition where L2 gives the naive solution. The mechanism is sparse binary codewords decoded by a near-pseudoinverse. A three-scalar description and hand-designed codes recover the trained network to about 1.1–1.2× loss, while per-entry encoder values and residual decoder structure remain unexplained.
record.recipe_differences: This is a computation task, not a reproduction of the original representation-superposition setup. It uses a 100-feature input, a 50-neuron ReLU layer, L4 training, and removes the residual connection from the compressed-computation model. The paper also reports an embedded variant.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome changes with loss exponent: exponent 2 gives the naive solution, while tested exponents above 2 give low per-feature-loss CV. Reduced embedding dimension weakens the effect. Designed-code performance also varies with code family and overlap minimization.

fits_no_version.finding: Given the trained codeword support, a three-scalar sparse binary code with a pseudoinverse decoder recovers the trained network to about 1.13× loss. Overlap-minimized designed biregular codes reach about 1.12×, while codes without overlap minimization sit at 1.67–1.90×.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Computation-in-superposition solutions in toy ReLU networks are well described by sparse binary codes over neurons with low pairwise overlap, decoded by a pseudoinverse.

record.problems: Evidence is from a toy elementwise-ReLU computation task at a stated sparsity of p = 0.02; the paper does not report a sparsity sweep. The reduced-dimension and larger-size checks measure only per-feature-loss CV, not the full code mechanism. Some comparisons are given as approximate ratios, and the code-geometry evidence does not establish how the result generalizes beyond this setup.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out.

untested.parts: The sparsity-dependent transition: sparsity is fixed at p=0.02. Also the original representation (autoencoding) task and geometry beyond codeword regularity and small overlaps.
Feature importance: all features are equally weighted, so the study does not test whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
Not tested: no LLMs and no SAEs.

missing.what: Encoder entries split into two clusters, on-code +0.34±0.06 and off-code −0.02±0.01, which defines the codewords; the embedded model matches.
Swap-test pass rate in the embedded model is 99.9%, and its decoder–pseudoinverse cosine is 0.996.
Load balancing: neurons in more codewords have lower on-code values (r ≈ −0.82).

record.verdict_notes: The tranche is changed from T2 to T3: this is a new computation setting, not a different method on the original representation question. The designed-code and ansatz rows (R10–R15) and the baselines (R4, R5) are the study's own constructions or comparators, so they are unlinked from the versions. The loss exponent was chosen by the authors to elicit the solution; readers should weigh that superposition appears only under non-L2 losses here.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests sparse-feature computation in a toy network, including shared codewords and some geometry. It does not vary feature sparsity, and therefore does not test a sparsity-dependent transition. Its focus is computation, not whether representation-superposition results generalize to other tasks.

The bottlenecked network shares neurons across feature codewords. The study does not vary feature importance or test whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while less important ones share.
The study does not test other causes of polysemanticity apart from capacity sharing in its toy computation task.
No LLM feature-spreading or SAE results are reported.
No SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonicality is tested.
The study identifies codewords over neurons but does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: axis-aligned single-hidden-layer ReLU network
rows.operation_detail: Train with L2 loss and measure coefficient of variation (CV) of per-feature MSE.
rows.measure: CV of per-feature MSE across the 100 features
rows.uncertainty: Across seeds, CV varies by at most 0.003 throughout the exponent sweep.
rows.note: The text describes the L2 solution as learning half the features and ignoring the rest, rather than spreading error evenly.
rows.check: Also bears on V2. Under L2, the same width bottleneck yields the naive solution: half the features are handled, the rest ignored, with no sharing. So capacity pressure alone did not produce shared neurons here.

rows.subject: axis-aligned single-hidden-layer ReLU network

rows.measure: Mean slope of output at the active feature's index
rows.uncertainty: The 5–95% band across features is too narrow to see.
rows.note: The paper attributes the under-shoot to interference from overlapping codewords.
rows.check: The slope of 0.81 is not a weak superposition effect. It is the interference signature the authors attribute to overlapping codewords, which is consistent with V1, so the state is observed rather than partial.

relationships.condition: Loss exponent >2 (L2.5–L8), p=0.02, 100 features/50 neurons, axis-aligned and embedded; also the 1000/500 scale-up
relationships.reason: Per-feature error is spread evenly (CV 0.028–0.046, 0.031 embedded, 0.06 at 1000/500). Each feature has a sparse codeword of 5–7 neurons in a near-biregular code with small overlaps. Swap tests decode correctly in 100% of cases, and the decoder is close to the pseudoinverse (0.996). See R2, R3, R6, R7, R8, R9, R16, R17, R20.
relationships.display_finding: Per-feature error was spread evenly (CV 0.028–0.046, 0.031 embedded, 0.06 at 1000/500), and each feature had a sparse codeword of 5–7 neurons in a near-biregular code with small overlaps. Swap tests decoded correctly in 100% of cases, and the decoder was close to the pseudoinverse (0.996).
